hook: Marcus, 34, twisted his knee in a basketball game and tore a C-shaped cartilage pad inside it, a meniscus. The same week he cut his forearm on a car door. The cut closed in ten days. His surgeon warns that the inner part of the meniscus tear will probably never heal on its own. Both injuries hit connective tissue. The difference comes down to what each tissue is made of and whether blood vessels run through it.

prereq.q: Which is the fluid part of blood?
prereq.why: Plasma is the liquid part of blood, mostly water with dissolved salts, nutrients and proteins. Red cells, white cells and platelets are suspended in it.

prereq.q: A cell that can divide and then become several different kinds of specialized cell is called what?
prereq.why: A stem cell can divide to make more of itself and can differentiate into specialized cells. Fully differentiated cells, such as red blood cells, have already specialized.

prereq.q: Which of the four primary tissue types is made of tightly packed cells with almost no material between them?
prereq.why: Epithelium is sheets of cells packed edge to edge, held by cell junctions. The connective type is the opposite: few cells in a lot of material between them.

chain.effect: Oxygen and nutrients reach its chondrocytes only by diffusing through the matrix from vessels outside it.

chain.cause: Diffusion through a thick, dense matrix is slow.
chain.effect: Chondrocytes are few, spread out and slow to divide or build new matrix.

chain.cause: After a tear, only a few slow cells with a poor supply are near the damage.
chain.effect: New matrix is laid down very slowly, and the inner part of a torn meniscus, farthest from any vessel, often never fills in.

chain.cause: Bone, by contrast, is full of blood vessels that deliver cells and nutrients to a break.
chain.effect: A broken bone usually heals in weeks, while torn cartilage may need surgery.

ideas: Connective tissue has relatively few cells scattered through a large amount of extracellular matrix (extra- = outside), the nonliving material the cells make and release around themselves. The matrix has two parts, a watery gel called ground substance and protein fibers, and it gives each connective tissue its properties.

Collagen fibers (kolla = glue, -gen = producing) are thick, white ropes of your most abundant protein: flexible but barely stretchy, and very strong when pulled. Elastic fibers stretch and snap back, and reticular fibers form delicate nets.

Fibroblasts (fibro- = fiber, -blast = builder) are the most common cells in connective tissue proper, and they make the fibers and ground substance. Macrophages (macro- = large, phag- = eat) are large cells that engulf bacteria, dead cells and debris by phagocytosis.

Loose connective tissue has few, loosely woven fibers and plenty of ground substance. It has three types: areolar tissue, the packing under most epithelia; adipose tissue, packed with adipocytes (adip- = fat) that each store a droplet of triglyceride; and reticular tissue, a net of reticular fibers that supports soft organs.

Dense connective tissue is packed with thick collagen fibers and has little ground substance. In dense regular tissue the bundles run in parallel, so it is strong along one line; it forms tendons (muscle to bone), ligaments (bone to bone) and aponeuroses, broad flat sheets of tendon. In dense irregular tissue they run in many directions, like felt, resisting pull from any side, as in your dermis.

Cartilage is a firm, avascular matrix made by chondrocytes (chondr- = cartilage). Hyaline cartilage (hyalos = glass), the most common, caps bone ends at joints with a smooth surface. Fibrocartilage mixes cartilage with thick collagen bundles, so it cushions and also resists pulling, as in intervertebral discs and knee menisci. Elastic cartilage holds many elastic fibers, so it bends and snaps back, as in your ear flap.

Mesenchyme (mes- = middle, -enchyme = poured-in tissue) is loose embryonic connective tissue: star-shaped stem cells in a watery ground substance with few fibers. As mesenchymal cells divide and differentiate, they become fibroblasts, fat cells, chondrocytes and the cells that build bone.

misconception.wrong: Blood can't be a connective tissue, because it is a liquid with no fibers.
misconception.right: Connective tissue is defined by cells scattered in a large amount of extracellular matrix. Blood fits. Plasma is its liquid matrix, and its fiber-forming protein is there all along in dissolved form; it turns into threads when a blood clot forms.

summary: Connective tissue is cells scattered in a large extracellular matrix of ground substance and fibers: collagen fibers resist pulling, elastic fibers stretch and recoil, and reticular fibers form nets. Fibroblasts build the matrix, and macrophages engulf debris. Loose connective tissue (areolar, adipose, reticular) cushions, fills, stores fat and supports soft organs. Dense regular tissue forms tendons, ligaments and aponeuroses; dense irregular tissue forms the dermis and organ capsules. Cartilage (hyaline, fibrocartilage, elastic) is avascular and heals poorly; bone is mineralized and well supplied. Blood is a fluid connective tissue with plasma as its matrix. Most of these arise from mesenchyme, which comes mainly from the embryo's middle layer.
